source: Global Burden of Disease Study 2019 (GBD 2019) - ADHD Analysis
citation: Cortese S, Song M, Farhat LC, et al. Incidence, prevalence, and global burden of ADHD from 1990 to 2019 across 204 countries: data, with critical re-analysis, from the Global Burden of Disease study. Mol Psychiatry. 2023;28(12):4823-4830. doi:10.1038/s41380-023-02228-3
methodology_note: GBD uses statistical modeling and imputation for countries without direct data. This analysis includes authors' critical re-analysis of the GBD data.

global_estimates_2019.gbd_mortality_assumption: Zero (GBD assumed no mortality from ADHD)

sex_distribution.note: Males have approximately 2.5x higher rates than females, stable from 1990-2019

pre_data_2013_prevalence_in_children_ado.conclusion: GBD may have substantially underestimated ADHD prevalence by roughly 2x in children/adolescents

authors_reanalysis_findings.income_level_difference: No significant differences in prevalence between low/middle-income and high-income countries in actual data (unlike GBD estimates)
authors_reanalysis_findings.adhd_related_mortality: Meta-analytic evidence of significantly increased ADHD-related mortality due to unnatural causes, contradicting GBD's zero-mortality assumption

gbd_limitations: Reliance on data imputation for countries without direct data may underestimate prevalence
Zero mortality assumption for ADHD is questionable
Modeling approach may not capture true population-level variation
limitations_acknowledged.age_restriction: This is lifespan data, not adults-only. Adult-specific GBD estimates are not directly reported in this paper.

comparison_to_wmh.note: GBD prevalence (1.13% lifespan) is lower than WMH adult prevalence (3.4% for ages 18-44). This difference likely reflects: (1) different diagnostic approaches, (2) GBD modeling vs. actual survey data, (3) different age ranges, (4) GBD's more conservative estimation methodology.
